readingInstruction: Read Romans 4:1-25. Paul uses Abraham as a case study. Notice the timing of Abraham’s faith, and the kind of faith that Paul describes.
settingTheScene: Abraham was the Jewish people’s founding father. Rabbis often taught that Abraham was justified because of his obedience, including his willingness to offer Isaac. If Paul can show that Abraham was right with God by faith, the Jewish objections collapse and the Gentiles are brought in. Genesis 15:6 is the verse on which Paul builds, and he reads it with great care.
observation: “For what does the Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (4:3).
“And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (4:5).
“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (4:7).
“He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised” (4:11).
“Who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (4:17).
“Fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (4:21).
“Who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (4:25).
interpretation:
Paul starts with a question: what did Abraham find? If he was justified by works, he would have something to boast about, but not before God. The Scripture says that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness. Notice the verb “counted.” It is bookkeeping language. Righteousness was credited to his account, not earned.

Then Paul reasons from the timeline. When was Abraham counted righteous? Before or after circumcision? Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17. Abraham was justified long before he was circumcised, and long before the law of Moses. Circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness he already had by faith. The consequence is wide: Abraham is the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness may be counted to them as well, and the father of the circumcised who also walk in the footsteps of his faith. Jew and Gentile are in the same family on the same terms.

The promise to Abraham did not come through the law, since law brings wrath, but through the righteousness of faith. “That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring.” This is a central point for understanding the covenants. The Abrahamic promise, that Abraham would be the father of many nations and heir of the world, is fulfilled in Christ, and all who share his faith are his children.

Abraham’s faith is described with care. God had promised him a son, but he and Sarah were old; Abraham’s body was as good as dead, and Sarah’s womb was barren. Yet “no unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.” He believed in a God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.” The faith that justifies is trust in the promise-keeping God, who raises the dead.

And the account was written for us. “It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.” The cross dealt with our sin; the resurrection is God’s public declaration that the payment was accepted. Abraham looked ahead to the promise; we look back to the resurrection. The object of faith is the same God, the one who raises the dead.
connection: Genesis 12:1-3, 15:1-6, and 17:1-14 are the Abrahamic narratives. Genesis 22 is the offering of Isaac. Galatians 3:6-9 and 3:26-29 make the same argument. Hebrews 11:8-19 describes Abraham’s faith. James 2:21-24 views Abraham’s works as evidence of his faith. Psalm 32 is the psalm David wrote. Isaiah 51:1-2 calls Israel to look to Abraham. Luke 1:73-75 speaks of the oath sworn to Abraham. Romans 1:4 and 8:11 connect the resurrection with justification and life.
application:
Compare Abraham’s faith with your own. What promise of God are you called to trust, even when it seems impossible?

Give glory to God today out loud. Faith grows by giving glory.

Thank God that the resurrection of Jesus is proof the payment was accepted.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for counting faith as righteousness.
Tell him what promise you are trusting him for.
Ask him to strengthen your faith like Abraham’s.
